doc.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Inspiration from church music, and losing a symphonic piece he never wrote down
summary: His writing draws on church music and blues; in college he heard a whole wind-ensemble piece in his head over three days, did not write it down, and lost it; he now writes everything down.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Where does your inspiration come from for writing new music?

Oh different things. It could be life experiences. I grew up in the church down south, I was in church every Sunday whether I wanted to be or not. I’d really like to do a Gospel album. I recorded a record on Cris Cross called “The Gospel Truth,” which was hymns and spirituals and a couple of original compositions. But it depends. It comes from many things. But mainly things that are blues based and the feeling I guess of the music of the church. And I think it’s intertwined in many different things. And sometimes I just am walking around, I hear things and I start to sing. And I learned a very important lesson when I was in college. I write everything down now. Because if you don’t, I think it’s very mysterious how this music thing works in terms of new music coming to you. It was, I’ll never forget it. I was playing in a symphonic band and I said I want to write a piece of symphonic or wind ensemble music. And it was just clear to me as day. And it took place over a three day period. I said oh, this is the thing. I was in college, taking a music course, and we were studying, I forget, Stravinsky or someone. And talking about theme and variations. A theme and how to develop a theme. And I said I’m going to write a piece of this music. And it was the spring season when we have concert band. And I hear the French horn part, I heard the trumpet parts, I heard all the percussion parts, and I said the first day, and the second day it was like oh yeah. And I didn’t write it down because it was just clear and just fresh in my mind. And the third day I was on the bus going somewhere and I said, oh yeah, this is how I can end the piece. And I said, you know I felt like it would be a great piece of music but who knows. But the thing is on the fourth day it was gone. And it was strange. And I could remember fragments of it, where just the day before I could hear the whole piece from beginning to end. My first symphonic piece of music. And I said oh man, just wow. And then like two, maybe like two years later I was riding in the car listening to a classical radio station and a piece of music I had never heard before, I found myself singing along with it. And I said I was baffled. So I never, and one other instance where it happened, it wasn’t my music but a piece of Wynton Marsalis’ music. We were playing from “In This House On This Morning” and we recorded the music and it had not come out yet. And we were on a tour © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
